As the [ADD LINK]Annual Average Temperature feature explains, increasing concentrations of heat-trapping greenhouse gases in the atmosphere are causing average temperatures at the Earth’s surface to rise. The increases may vary by season, however, and so do the impacts. Changing winter temperatures directly influence the amount of snow that falls and accumulates, amount of seasonal snowpack, timing of snowmelt runoff, loss of soil moisture through evapotranspiration, and amount of time that lakes are frozen. These impacts matter for water supplies, winter traditions, and local economies that depend on winter recreation. Warming in other seasons can also affect daily life in various ways, such as agriculture, pollen allergies, heating and cooling, or the timing of life cycle events that are important for plants and animals.

This feature builds on EPA’s Seasonal Temperature indicator by presenting projections of average surface temperature for the four seasons within the contiguous United States.
